paras: The lynching of Theo Calloway was the killing of a Black man accused of murdering a white man, Mitchell Gresham, by about 200 armed and masked men who took him from the Lowndes County jail at Hayneville, Alabama, on the night of March 29, 1888, and hanged him in front of the courthouse. A Montgomery dispatch about the lynching ran in papers from Maine to Texas within a week, and the Huntsville Gazette called it "shameful" and urged punishment of the mob. In May, reports of an armed clash between the county sheriff's posse and Black residents traced the trouble to the lynching.

According to the Montgomery dispatch, Calloway and Gresham had quarreled over a rubber coat a few days before the lynching. The dispatch said that Gresham and his brother met Calloway on the public road while he carried a shotgun, and that when Gresham asked what he meant to do with it, Calloway fired and killed him instantly. The shooting took place near Sandy Ridge in Lowndes County, and Calloway was held in the county jail at Hayneville to await a preliminary trial.

At about midnight on Thursday, March 29, some 200 armed and masked men rode into Hayneville, went to the jail and demanded Calloway. They forced the jailer to surrender the keys, took Calloway from the cell where he was sleeping, and hanged him from the limb of a tree in front of the courthouse. His body was riddled with bullets and left hanging until the next day, when it was turned over to his parents, who had come to Hayneville for the preliminary trial; they took it back to Sandy Ridge for burial. The men then rode out of town, and the dispatches said nothing was known of their identity "except that they were friends of the murdered man."

Writing on April 14, the Huntsville Gazette praised an unspecified "action" by Governor Seay concerning the lynching as "a right step in the right direction" but argued that it should not stop at "mere 'inquiry.'" A brief printed in May by the Willimantic Journal said the governor had asked the sheriff of Lowndes County for an account of the lynching and that the sheriff "replied practically that his excellency might mind his own business." Beyond these two reports, no account of an inquest, arrests or indictments of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

On May 4, according to a special dispatch to the Advertiser carried from Montgomery, the sheriff's posse arrested fifteen Black men at Sandy Ridge and then fought an armed group of Black residents; two white men were reported wounded and several Black men killed, and troops were sent from Montgomery. The dispatch said that "ever since the lynching of Calloway in March, the negroes have been threatening vengeance," and the Memphis Appeal wrote that the renewed trouble was believed to have its origin in the lynching. These accounts came from the sheriff and white correspondents, and the Appeal itself called the telegraphed news "meagre and conflicting."

The first reports, on March 31, were versions of a Montgomery dispatch: a short one ran in the Richmond Dispatch as "An Alabama Lynching" and in the Savannah Morning News as "A Murderer Lynched," naming Calloway as the man "who murdered young Mitchell Gresham" without qualification. The longer version in the New York Sun, reprinted in the Maysville Evening Bulletin on April 2, began "Judge Lynch got in his work" and said the mob had "avenged one of the most dastardly, cold-blooded murders in the criminal history of the State."

Condensed briefs in the Interior Journal, the National Tribune, the Kanabec County Times and the Griggs Courier called Calloway "a murderer" or "a negro murderer," some placing the jail at "Sayneville" or Montgomery.

The Huntsville Gazette was the only paper in the coverage to condemn the lynching outright, calling Judge Lynch "a menance to the peace and happiness of any community" and demanding "swift justice" for "the outlaws who take the law into their own hands." When the May clash was reported, the Savannah Morning News headed it "A Race War in Alabama," while the Annapolis Evening Capital warned that "lynching negroes down South is likely to result seriously to the whites."

Reports differed on the victim's name, printed as Theo. or Theodore Calloway in most papers but also as "Colloway" and "Galloway," and one reprint put the mob at 300 rather than 200. The March 30 dispatches, the "Thursday night" version and the Huntsville Gazette placed the lynching on the night of March 29, while condensed briefs gave the 30th.

accounts.label: Montgomery wire (long)
accounts.gist: About 200 armed, masked men rode in at midnight, forced the jailer to give up the keys and hanged Calloway; it recounts the Gresham shooting as fact and says the mob avenged a 'dastardly' murder.

accounts.label: Huntsville Gazette editorial
accounts.gist: Called the lynching 'shameful', praised Gov. Seay's action and urged 'swift justice' for the mob rather than mere inquiry.

accounts.label: May reports from Lowndes
accounts.gist: Black residents had threatened vengeance since the lynching, and this led to a May 4 clash with the sheriff's posse; the governor had asked the sheriff for an account of the lynching and been rebuffed.
